newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Protestant leader in prison visit.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Protestant leader in prison visit.

text.p: David Trimble, leader of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British Protestant party, will press jailed Loyalist guerrillas on Friday to continue backing a two-year truce, party sources said on Thursday.

They said Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), would pay a visit to the top-security Maze prison to talk to Loyalists imprisoned for security offences in their 27-year war to keep the province British.

Trimble would press the Loyalists to continue backing the truce by their activists still at large and not to avenge a return to violence in February by Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, they said.
"They must continue down the road to peace. There must be no going back to violence," said UUP Honorary Secretary Jeffrey Donaldson, who will accompany Trimble to the Maze.
Trimble's party is the biggest voice of the 60 percent Protestant majority which wants the province to stay British and resist Catholic Irish nationalists who want it reunited under Dublin's rule.
The sources said Trimble would meet members of one branch of the Loyalists, the outlawed Ulster Defence Association, which withdrew its support for a two-year peace process this month.
Loyalists are demanding early prison releases to reward them for backing the truce and maintaining their side of an uneasy peace which has existed since 1994.
Britain has publicly ruled out any such amnesty saying the Loyalists and their IRA foes are common crimininals, not political detainees, and can only expect normal terms of remIssion.
Trimble's visit will take place one day before the UUP's annual party conference amid new fears of a return the violence which killed 3,200 people before IRA and Loyalist truces in 1994.

The views of jailed Loyalists were seen as crucial in shaping the 1994 ceasefire which permitted small political parties representing their views to be admitted to Belfast peace talks which started in June.
The Loyalists said in October 1994 that they would stand by their truce so long as the IRA maintained its own ceasefire.
The IRA bombing of Britain's army headquarters in Northern Ireland last week has raised fears that the Loyalist truce will crumble and that its militia will seek to avenge the attack.
The Combined Loyalist Military Command, an umbrella group representing the outlawed UDA and Ulster Volunteer Force, is reported to have met to consider its next move but has issued no statement.
